messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mariam is a 78-year-old widow who has supported herself for years through pottery, working alone in a small studio behind her house. The assault happened there one winter evening after she had stayed late glazing bowls for a local market. She heard a noise near the back door and assumed it was the wind rattling the frame, but when she turned, a man was already inside. What has remained with her is not a coherent story so much as a set of stark images: the dark shape in the doorway, the shine of metal from a tool he carried, the flash of her own face in the studio mirror as he shoved past her, wide-eyed and disbelieving. Since then, when the memory comes, it does not feel like something past. It arrives without warning and as pictures, so vivid that she feels for a moment that she is back in the studio with him entering again.

In the weeks after the assault, Mariam had come to believe that the world was simply dangerous and that safety could vanish in an instant. What frightened her most was how strongly her body still reacted even in daylight, in her own home, as if some part of her had not learned that the assault was over. She became convinced that if she let herself think directly about what happened, she would be overwhelmed and unable to manage it. From that belief, her habits began to narrow. She tried hard to push the assault out of mind whenever it surfaced. She started checking the locks on her doors and windows repeatedly before bed and again after she lay down. She also found herself looking into mirrors again and again, especially the one by the studio entrance, as if confirming what was behind her might prevent another attack.

Those same beliefs kept her body on alert. Because she now saw danger as everywhere, she listened constantly for signs that someone might be entering the house. At night she would wake suddenly and sit upright, certain she needed to check whether she was safe. Even when neighbors were nearby or her doors were bolted, she could not settle into ease. She described it as her nerves refusing to believe reassurance. That ongoing watchfulness fit with what she had come to think: that her body was an unreliable enemy, primed for danger whether or not danger was present.

The memories themselves deepened this conviction. An image of the doorway or of her own frightened face in the mirror would force its way into her mind while she was trimming clay or carrying finished pots to cool. In those moments she felt the assault was happening right now, and the intensity of that reliving seemed to prove to her that she was not truly safe and perhaps not truly recovering. Each episode confirmed her fear that thinking about the assault was dangerous in itself. If a memory could seize her so completely, she reasoned, then deliberately allowing it into her mind might undo her altogether.

Because the memories came this way, Mariam became more determined to manage them. She would stop herself mid-thought, turn on a light, check the back door, then check it again. In the studio she began using reflective surfaces to scan the room behind her, looking over her shoulder and then back into the mirror, trying to get ahead of the next image before it took hold. At home, when a memory burst in at bedtime, she got up to inspect windows and locks rather than remain in bed with the pictures. These rituals gave her a few moments of relief, but they also kept her attention fixed on the possibility of another intrusion.

Over months, that pattern hardened. The more she checked and scanned, the more real the danger felt to her. Repeatedly testing locks never led her to feel secure for long; instead it seemed to confirm that constant vigilance was necessary. Pushing thoughts away made them feel more potent when they returned. She had come to see her own reactions as evidence that the world remained unsafe and that she herself could not handle remembering. Her pottery changed as well. She stopped working after dusk, kept the studio door shut even in warm weather, and interrupted her work whenever a sound from the alley made her freeze and listen. Orders fell behind, and she felt ashamed when customers asked why pieces were not ready.

By the time she sought help, Mariam was exhausted from broken nights and from the strain of never relaxing. She said she was tired of living as if someone were always about to come through the door, and tired of being ambushed by pictures that made the past feel present. What finally brought her in was the fear that her life had shrunk to locks, mirrors, and listening. What she wants most is to be able to work in her studio again without feeling that every sound means danger, but she is deeply afraid that if she stops guarding herself, the assault will happen all over again.
